accuracy.reason: Cards accurately separate acceptance, effect, broker retirement, redelivery and retained-log progress; atomicity is explicitly restricted to the database. Diagrams preserve both acknowledgement boundaries and independent groups.

evidence.quote: That transaction protects its database effects. It does not make an external email or payment atomic, or turn delivery into a universal exactly-once guarantee.

mechanisms.reason: All eight objectives have causal mechanisms: handoff, save-before-ack crash window, unique transactional ID, bounded retries, per-entity serialization, backlog arithmetic, offsets and request dependency.

evidence.quote: Serialize effects per entity ID: keep later updates waiting while an earlier one runs or retries.

coherence.reason: Acceptance establishes responsibility; actors and crash boundaries lead to retry/order controls, finite buffering, independent consumption and sync/async choice. Prerequisites are supplied before application.

decisions.reason: Explains when callers can defer, visible status and operating costs, bounded concurrency/admission, poison isolation/replay and per-entity throughput versus ordering.

evidence.quote: Keep decisions synchronous when the next action requires their result.

clarity.reason: Definitions and examples explain rather than merely name mechanisms. Queue versus log, delivery versus completion and acceptance versus ready remain distinct throughout.

evidence.quote: This shortens the initial wait, not the work itself.

outcomes.reason: Cards 1/2/8 support API-producer/broker/worker roles, confirmed configured handoff, saved result before consumer ack, visible pending/ready/failed state, synchronous access decision and concrete costs. Learner covers all.

Card 3 supports post-commit redelivery, pre-effect acknowledgement loss, stable operation ID, durable unique transactional effect/duplicate record and no universal exactly-once delivery. Learner applies the credit scenario correctly.

Card 4 supports delayed retries with finite attempt/time budget, immediate isolation of unchanged permanent input, visible failed state, healthy-work protection and corrected duplicate-safe replay. Learner preserves unspecified numeric policy rather than inventing one.

Card 5 supports old effect finishing last and final quantity 5, delivery/completion distinction, per-item serialization across retries, independent item concurrency and hot-item throughput/wait cost. Learner includes dependency handling after dead-lettering.

Card 6 supports 120-80=40 growth, oldest-age completion risk, bounded saturated-store calls, visible throttling/rejection/deferral, finite retention/burst limits and conditional worker scaling. Learner transfers the different rates correctly.

Card 7 teaches competing distribution versus independent groups, within-group partition sharing, per-group offsets, nondeletion on progress, retention-limited replay and per-partition order without exactly-once effects. Learner covers each.

sourceChecks.claim: Microsoft async request-reply documents accepted versus completed status and deferred processing; visible terminal failure and caller dependency determine fit.
RabbitMQ confirms explicitly separates publisher acceptance from consumer delivery acknowledgements; neither spans an application database transaction. Diagram preserves those boundaries.

AWS idempotent APIs supports stable caller operation identity and ACID record/effect handling; RabbitMQ redelivery and the idempotent-consumer pattern support the described crash window and unique processed-ID transaction.
Microsoft retry guidance supports transient versus persistent failures, finite attempts/delays and idempotency; RabbitMQ dead-letter documentation supports isolation, not automatic repair.

Microsoft competing consumers warns ordering is not assured with concurrency and suggests ordered sessions; per-entity serialized effects prevent later completion overtaking earlier retries at a throughput cost.
Microsoft load leveling warns sustained producer excess grows latency, consumer scaling can overload dependencies, and size/retention are finite; both backlog subtractions are correct.

Kafka design documents independent consumer positions, partition assignment, retained records and offset-controlled replay. Position commits do not delete history or alone ensure external exactly-once effects.
Microsoft async request-reply supports status/result lifecycle and operating costs; deferral cannot remove a dependency on a completed authorization result.
